tagline.text: A brick Baroque church in Isabela with a unique cylindrical belfry

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Annafunan, Tumauini town, Isabela (St. Matthias Parish)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,500 (round-trip transport and meals from Tuguegarao)

children.text: Tumauini Church (St. Matthias Church) is a Spanish colonial church built of brick by Dominican priests in the 18th and 19th centuries. With its cylindrical belfry and intricate brick ornamentation, it is a National Cultural Treasure and a National Historic Landmark, and it is on the UNESCO Tentative List.
Tumauini Church is formally St. Matthias Parish, in the town of Tumauini, Isabela, within the Diocese of Ilagan. It stands in the middle of the Cagayan Valley, more than
460 km

north of Manila, between Ilagan City and Cabagan. Good stone is scarce in this area, so the church was built of fired red brick instead of the usual limestone or adobe, which makes it a rare example of brick Baroque among the Spanish-era churches of the Philippines. Compared with the famous
Paoay Church

, which gives a heavy impression with coral stone and brick and huge buttresses, Tumauini Church is smaller but gives a delicate impression, with ornament packed densely onto the brick, so comparing the two is fun.

The story begins in 1707, when the Dominican priest Francisco Nuñez built a light church of timber and nipa palm. In 1751 Tumauini separated from Cabagan and became its own parish. The present church was begun in 1783 by Fr. Domingo Forto, taken over in 1788 by Fr. Antonio Herrera, and completed in 1805. With three priests spanning more than 20 years of work, the church and belfry carry layered traces of different periods.

The face of the church is its facade. It has pseudo-Corinthian columns and niches, and its circular pediment is considered unique among the Spanish-era churches of the Philippines. The brick is carved with flowers, leaves, ovules and sunbursts, and this clay ornament is said to have been made with wooden molds crafted by artisans from Betis, Pampanga. Each brick carries a number marking where it should be laid, and some also bear dates, which hints at how the building was constructed. The white plaster finish is original, but weathering has exposed the red brick underneath in many places.

The church's most famous feature is the cylindrical belfry built in 1805. Its tiered shape and garland-like decoration have earned it the nickname of a wedding cake, and it is said to be the only cylindrical belfry of the Spanish colonial period in the Philippines. The bell has bullet holes and has never been recast. On the gospel side of the church, the ruins of the convent (clergy house) remain. The church was damaged in World War II but was faithfully reconstructed, keeping as much of what survived as possible. On February 24, 1989, the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) declared it a National Historic Landmark, and it is also a National Cultural Treasure. Since 2006 it has been on the UNESCO Tentative List as part of the "Baroque Churches of the Philippines (Extension)," together with the churches of Boljoon, Guiuan, Loboc and Lazi. On site, walk around the sides and back of the church as well as the facade and belfry to compare how the bricks were laid and which parts were restored.

This tiered round belfry, completed in 1805, is known as the only cylindrical belfry of the colonial period in the Philippines. The sharp contrast of white plaster and red brick makes it the most popular photo spot.

The facade is covered with flowers, leaves, ovules and sunbursts carved into brick. The clay ornament was made with wooden molds by artisans from Betis, Pampanga, so each pattern looks refined up close.
The curved pediment at the top of the facade, with its circular window, is considered unique among Spanish-era churches. The window is reported to have been renovated recently.
Numbers and dates are carved into the bricks, showing that each brick's place was planned before construction. It is fun to look for them on the lower parts of the wall.
In the Cagayan style, the facade is made of brick because adobe and good stone were hard to get. It is smaller than other Baroque churches, but its ornament is considered denser.
On the gospel side of the church, the remains of the clergy house let you imagine the size of the old convent. Because it is a ruin with exposed brick, check on site whether there are safety lines.

Since 2006 it has been on the tentative list as part of the "Baroque Churches of the Philippines (Extension)," which recognizes its conservation value. Please avoid touching it or leaning on it so you cause no damage.

The plaster finish is said to be original, but after long weathering it has peeled in places and exposed the red brick beneath. The feel of its age, left as it is, is both the charm of this church and its conservation challenge.

items.title: Half day from Tuguegarao
items.subtitle: The church and a loop around Ilagan

children.text: Take a van or bus from Tuguegarao to Tumauini town. The trip is reported to take about
1 hour
Get off in front of Puregold Tumauini and walk about two blocks from the main road to find the church and municipal hall.
Take your time looking at the brick ornament on the facade and the cylindrical belfry. The photos come out best in the morning, before the sun gets strong.
Walk around the side and back of the church to find the numbers carved on the bricks and the restored parts. Also look at the gospel-side wall where the convent ruins stand.
If the doors are open and no event such as a Mass or funeral is under way, look around the interior quietly. Check opening hours with the parish.
Have lunch in town and try a noodle dish such as pancit Cabagan, a specialty of the Isabela and Cagayan area.
Move on to Ilagan and visit other sights such as nearby churches and Fuyot Springs National Park, or return to Tuguegarao.
Opening hours and interior access are said to vary by day. It is safer to ask the parish in advance.
Look at colonial-era buildings in downtown Ilagan, such as Our Lady of Atocha Church.
Come down to Tumauini, see the church and have a meal.
If time remains, add natural sights near Ilagan, such as Fuyot Springs National Park.
Buses (Victory Liner, Five Star and others) run from Manila to Tuguegarao, taking about
8–9 hours
, with an air-conditioned fare of about ₱650 or more.

From Tuguegarao, take a UV Express van to Ilagan, or a Manila-bound bus, and get off in front of Puregold in Tumauini town. One source gave the van fare to Ilagan as about ₱60 and the travel time as about
1 hour
From Puregold, the church and municipal hall are about two blocks from the main road, within walking distance.
Bus fares and travel times differ by company, so check before you go. An overnight bus gets you to Tuguegarao at dawn, so you can make full use of the day.
Fly from Manila to Tuguegarao (TUG), then continue overland to Tumauini as above.
The nearest airport is Cauayan City Airport, which Cebu Pacific is reported to connect with Manila in about
1 hour 10 minutes
. From Cauayan, the van to Tumauini takes at least
1 hour
and costs about ₱50 or more.
Flight routes and schedules change often. Check before you leave.
The church is close to the main road, but if it is very hot you can take a tricycle.
From Santiago or Cordon, take a van bound for Tuguegarao and get off at Puregold Tumauini.
The Cagayan Valley is an area of very strong midday heat. The dry, relatively cool months of November–February are the most comfortable for walking around the church and town.
From March to May midday temperatures are high, so visit early in the morning, and during the rainy season and typhoon season from June to October, rain can make outdoor sightseeing inconvenient.

Around 10 AM, when the facade catches the sun, the depth of the brick ornament shows best, and in the late afternoon, as the sun gets lower, the red of the belfry deepens. Either way, avoid the midday hours around noon, when shadows are short, photos look flat and the heat is intense.

items.label: Meals
items.note: One meal at a restaurant in town

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.

Tumauini is a small town with few places to stay. The easiest plan is to stay in Tuguegarao or Ilagan and make a day trip. The church and municipal hall are about two blocks from the main road, so they are easy to find.
In town, the noodle dish pancit Cabagan, named after the neighboring town, is worth trying. Plan on about ₱80–150 per meal.

The Isabela and Cagayan area is known for noodle dishes such as pancit Cabagan, which originated in this region. After seeing the church, have a light meal at a restaurant along the main road, and if you need more variety in food and lodging, it is better to move on to Tuguegarao or Ilagan. Many places in town take cash, so bring plenty of small bills.
During events such as a Mass or funeral, watch quietly and refrain from taking photos.
Early morning gives better photos and avoids the midday heat.
Interior access varies from day to day and it may be closed, so check with the parish first.
The brick and plaster are fragile, so do not lean on or touch them.
Getting off in front of Puregold Tumauini makes it easy to find your way.
Combining the visit with Ilagan makes the half-day trip richer.
After seeing the facade, go around to the side to look at the convent ruins and the tiered structure of the belfry together, which makes it easier to understand.
The numbers and dates on the bricks can only be seen up close, so walk slowly and look for them.
The church is a cultural property, but it is also a parish where services are still held. Entry may be restricted during events.
We could not confirm opening hours or interior access rules. Ask the parish before you go.
Midday heat is intense, so bring a hat, water and sunscreen.
The conservation condition is fragile, so do not touch the walls or decoration.
Road conditions can worsen in the rainy season, so check the weather before traveling.
Depending on restoration or repair work, some areas may be closed. Follow the signs and the parish caretaker.

The central city of Cagayan, serving as the starting and returning base for a church visit. Its airport, bus terminals, lodging and restaurants are all here, so it also works well to stay one night and visit the church the next day.

A national park in Ilagan City that fits well on the same day as the church. A travel blogger toured this park in the morning and then moved on to Tumauini. Check opening status and entry conditions locally.
A limestone cave attraction in Peñablanca, south of Tuguegarao, good to combine as a separate trip.
